item.title: Easy to integrate, compliant by design: Bringing the Swiss Franc to Google Cloud Universal Ledger
item.description:
Every day, countless financial transactions are interrupted by slow, expensive, and inflexible conventional payment systems. As a result, public commercial stablecoins like Tether, USDC, and PayPal USD have become increasingly popular by making it easy to move money efficiently with instant, 24/7 blockchain settlement.

Yet major regulated banks have largely kept such transactions at arm’s length; for these financial institutions, reserve-backed public stablecoins present numerous risks, including strict capital and liquidity requirements and unmanageable regulatory and operational uncertainty.

Indeed, banks don't want to adopt existing stablecoins. Instead, they need the speed and efficiency of tokenized currency built on the trusted economic foundations they’ve nurtured over years or even decades in business. That’s why many are now turning to Google Cloud Universal Ledger (GCUL). Rather than channeling public stablecoins, GCUL provides the secure infrastructure banks need to issue and settle tokenized deposits. That brings real-time, 24/7 programmable payments into commercial bank money while satisfying regulators and without disrupting core banking operations.

For many banks, this is a compelling vision, but adopting new payment technology and integrating it with core banking systems can seem to bank CTOs like a daunting undertaking. That’s particularly true as they face mounting demands for the engineering resources that keep their businesses running while also striving to stay compliant with new regulations. But with a blockchain purpose-built for financial services like GCUL, this is anything but a herculean task.

Looking to expand its offerings for an increasingly global clientele, Switzerland’s Crypto Finance Group wanted to show it could deploy payment innovations like this in just weeks. That was its inspiration for launching a digital payments infrastructure pilot that enabled instant account-to-account transfers between customers of two Swiss banks on the GCUL network. The pilot, which was designed to operate within one of the world's most demanding financial security frameworks, provided a blueprint for how any commercial bank can build on Google Cloud technology to fundamentally modernize its payment operations.

Pain points in today's payments landscape

In recent years, there’s been a marked proliferation of tokenized payment methods. But stablecoins have transformed this previously niche technology, by effectively resolving some of traditional finance’s most enduring pain points, such as weekend transfer blackouts, direct transfers without correspondent banks, and fast settlement rails. Stablecoins also limit the frustrations caused by opaque cross-border transactions, where fragmented compliance checks can leave legitimate payments in extended and unexplained limbo and without a path to clear or timely resolution.

Still, commercial banks have been reluctant to offer popular reserve-backed stablecoins from permissionless blockchains to their customers despite their retail popularity. That’s because they come with numerous challenges to smooth and secure operations: an uncertain regulatory status, compliance issues around anonymous accounts, gas fees, and the scalability limitations of layer 1 blockchain technology. But perhaps banks’ biggest concerns about stablecoins is that they create a problematic economic disconnect — giving customers access to reserve-backed stablecoins reduces reserves and, as a recent McKinsey study found, banks’ ability to lend.

As a result, many banks are trying to figure out how to offer their customers the benefits of stablecoins — high speed, low cost, 24/7 availability, and programmability — without introducing problems often associated with existing reserve-backed stablecoins, such as regulatory issues, poor throughput performance, negative influence on bank reserves, and potentially no yield participation.

Solution proposal

Realizing this vision means modernized payments architectures must seamlessly and instantly enable individuals and institutions to transfer bank-held assets to accounts at any target bank. Orchestrating this shared ecosystem requires central entities to establish the governing rulebook, enforce issuance limits, and manage network-wide settlement parameters. During its pilot, Crypto Finance assumed this role, which within GCUL is known as the “currency operator.”

In this position, Crypto Finance can configure the network for either instant or deferred settlement. This choice is analogous to traditional banking: instant settlement acts like real-time gross settlement, where transactions settle individually and immediately and require high liquid reserves. In contrast, deferred settlement operates like netting, where payments are accumulated and offset and only periodically settle the net difference. For the pilot, Crypto Finance chose to adopt deferred settlement, in which GCUL manifests capital efficiency. In this way, clients enjoy instant transfers while banks conserve liquidity through periodic settlement.

Concept validation

To demonstrate instant, bi-directional account-to-account transfers on GCUL, Crypto Finance orchestrated a pilot with two digital token issuers, a Swiss digital asset bank, and a Swiss B2B transaction bank. Crypto Finance established the rulebook for interactions between the participant banks, such as interbank settlement, integration with traditional SIC payment rails, and AML/compliance protocols. Although some backend steps still needed manual intervention, Crypto Finance’s pilot proved that fully automated, cross-institution integration is feasible and established a generalized architecture that can scale to virtually any asset class.

Robustness and performance

A temporary pilot is one thing; moving into live client transactions carrying legal liability brings a whole new set of operational challenges. Live payment rails are considered critical infrastructure that demands security and availability. GCUL addresses these needs through redundancy between geographically distributed nodes operating on an enterprise-grade consensus model, ensuring reliability. Deploying client workloads on Google Cloud provides that enterprise-grade foundation and allows financial institutions to pair the highly resilient GCUL network with secure-by-design infrastructure, encryption at rest and in transit, and robust access controls that satisfy many of banks’ common regulatory, privacy, and data sovereignty mandates. While some banks may consider integrating their systems with fully public and permissionless blockchains, this approach introduces severe regulatory hurdles, anonymity risks, unpredictable gas fees, and low throughput. These are all roadblocks that in the past would have significantly delayed the pilot or rendered it a non-starter.

Ease of integration

The pilot's implementation, with systems integration completed in under three months, was compartmentalized across dedicated Google Cloud projects per participant. The currency operator, Crypto Finance, connected specialized components to a dedicated GCUL API. The first was a role admin service that controls account managers and token managers on the network. Next, it implemented a settlement registry to record when periodic off-ledger settlement between participant banks has occurred once a predefined threshold is reached. Finally, a cloud key management service (KMS) stored the currency operator keys to sign transactions.

At the same time, participant banks connected their core banking systems to their own GCUL API instances. But these participant banks don’t need a large Google Cloud footprint. Instead, they can connect to GCUL nodes via Remote Procedure Call from their existing on-premise deployments and manage private key material through solutions other than KMS. Regardless of the setup, transactions are seamlessly routed to the shared global GCUL nodes.

Whether GCUL is exposed to a bank’s client or used merely as a bank backend is entirely at the integrating institution’s discretion. The banks participating in the pilot chose the latter, utilizing the ledger to upgrade their backend infrastructure. With GCUL under the hood, they improved intra-day transaction performance and provided customers with the user experience they were already accustomed to.

Regulatory compliance and governance by design

To join the Swiss Franc currency network on GCUL, participants must have regulatory licenses that let them perform third-party transfers and issue commercial bank money. Crucially, features like token and account management are not rigid network-wide limitations. Instead, they rely entirely on the currency operator and its specific rulebook. This standardizes fees, limits, settlement times, and technical configurations.

Managing counterparty risk is central to this governance. Rather than relying on unscalable bilateral agreements or complex clearinghouse default waterfalls, GCUL mitigates risk through these currency operator-enforced issuance limits.

It’s important to distinguish GCUL’s broader feature set from the concrete pilot setup. In the pilot, both participating banks operated with conservative initial limits based on their credit ratings in order to safely prove the architecture. But beyond the pilot, the network frees up capital by periodically netting outstanding obligations, which frees banks from having to fund and settle every transaction.

Looking ahead, risk management can be further innovated. One clever future enhancement would be to allow participants to dynamically increase their issuance limits by committing digital assets as collateral in segregated accounts, using solutions like Crypto Finance’s AnchorNote pledging solution. These assets could then be used to instantly settle outstanding street-side obligations, virtually eliminating counterparty risk without tying up traditional liquidity reserves.

The future

While Crypto Finance’s pilot was designed to focus on domestic commercial bank money transfers in Switzerland, GCUL's programmable architecture and high-performance smart contract language, GCULpy, are paving the way for deeper innovation. As institutions like Crypto Finance scale their use of GCUL, the network can expand to support real-time cross-currency settlement, automated foreign exchange, and dynamic collateral management involving tokenized digital assets. And looking further ahead, this infrastructure has laid the groundwork for next-generation financial services that range from point-of-sale payments to autonomous, AI-driven agentic payments.

The pilot proved that deploying high-performance, blockchain-based payment rails doesn’t mean compromising on strict regulatory compliance or core banking stability. By combining the high-throughput of GCUL with a secure, API-driven integration architecture, commercial banks can offer stablecoin-like speed to their customers while seamlessly preserving their capital efficiency. Ultimately, this compliant-by-design approach targets the operational bottlenecks of traditional finance while mitigating the inherent risks and complexities of public blockchains.

To learn how your institution can build on this blueprint to fundamentally upgrade your operational payments infrastructure, contact Google Cloud Sales to explore the Google Cloud Universal Ledger.

The team would also like to thank Phil Dettwiler, Andras Miklos, Ignazio Pollina, and Ozan Kizildogan at Crypto Finance and Googlers Chris Esch, Ishan Singh, Olena Clayton, and Stathis Onasoglou for their contributions.

item.title: Google Cloud expands model choice and flexibility, bringing OpenAI models to customers
item.description:
Google Cloud has always been defined by choice, enterprise-grade governance, and market-leading price-performance. Key to the foundation of openness and choice is giving customers flexibility to run agentic workloads across their choice of models and infrastructure to achieve the right balance of cost, capability, and performance. Today, we are expanding that foundation by launching OpenAI models in Google Cloud’s model garden.

Google Cloud is now the only hyperscale cloud provider offering access to all three leading closed source LLMs, alongside more than 200 first-party, third-party, and open models on a unified enterprise AI platform.

The right model for every workload

Modern enterprise AI requires matching each workload to the right model rather than relying on a single model for every task. By adding OpenAI’s newest models to model garden, we are giving teams options across the full spectrum of enterprise workloads. For OpenAI models:

  • GPT-6 Astra: Designed for demanding work across coding, computer use, professional tasks, and scientific research.
  • GPT-6.1 Sol: Near-Astra intelligence at lower cost across agentic coding, computer use, and professional work.
  • GPT-6 Luna: A fast, cost-efficient model for everyday work at scale.

Using the platform, customers can dynamically select and swap the optimal model for any use case based on performance, latency, and cost efficiency without architectural lock-in or separate vendor contracts. Developers gain the freedom to build with hundreds of choices in model garden. Because OpenAI models are transacted directly through Google Cloud Marketplace, all usage appears on a single Google Cloud invoice, draws down existing cloud commitments, and counts toward Flexible Savings Plans (FSP) across model providers.

Built-in data governance and enterprise security

Scaling generative AI should never require compromising on compliance or security. Built from the ground up for enterprise governance, the Gemini platform is trusted by leading global organizations today. We ensure that running any third-party or OpenAI workload meets the most rigorous enterprise standards:

  • Strict data perimeters: Customer prompts, context, and outputs remain entirely within your designated data perimeter and are never used to train foundation models, with Zero Data Retention (ZDR) options available coming soon.
  • Isolated access boundaries: OpenAI models run on dedicated Google Cloud infrastructure with Confidential Compute coming soon. All queries are routed through hardened, isolated gateways, ensuring data transit remains strictly within Google Cloud's secure environment and third-party model providers have no unauthorized access to your cloud environment.
  • Unified auditing and identity: Every agent and model interaction operates under an authenticated identity, giving IT administrators end-to-end visibility, VPC Service Controls protection, and unified audit logging across their entire enterprise footprint.

“Helping customers put AI to work across their enterprise content requires leading models backed by strong security and rigorous compliance standards,” said Yashodha Bhavnani, VP of AI Products at Box. “By using OpenAI models through Google Cloud, we will be able to give customers access to OpenAI’s frontier AI models alongside Google Cloud’s security and compliance capabilities, enabling them to get more value from their enterprise content. This is a step toward operating more efficiently as we bring AI to customers.”

Getting started

OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-6 Luna models are rolling out now in private preview to select enterprise customers in Google Cloud’s model garden, with more coming soon. Starting today, customers can build with these models through our APIs and connect their local Codex CLI and Desktop workflows directly to our Gemini platform for inference. Please use this form to express interest.

Coming soon, OpenAI models will be available in Google Cloud’s Gemini for business and Google Antigravity, providing enterprise customers and developers with model choice flexibility and the best model for each task.

item.title: Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 are now available in Google Antigravity
item.description:
Whether you are iterating on a quick bug fix or planning a complex migration, different tasks call for different models.

In keeping with Google Cloud's commitment to an open ecosystem and to give developers the right model for every job, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 are now available in Google Antigravity for Google Cloud customers. Claude Opus 5.5 is built for complex work while Claude Sonnet 5.5 is a faster, lower-cost complement.

Once enabled by an administrator, developers can select Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 directly from the model picker. Administrators can also select Google’s Gemini models, including Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 4 Argon. The models apply across Antigravity 2.0, Antigravity CLI and our recently released Antigravity IDE extensions for VS Code, JetBrains IntelliJ, and Visual Studio. This lets you choose the right model for the job, under a unified enterprise billing and security boundary.

In this post, we’ll share two engineering patterns for building in Antigravity using these models. To view the entire list of models supported in Antigravity across subscriptions, see our documentation here.

Multi-model engineering patterns in Antigravity

Having multiple model families available inside the same agent harness unlocks practical multi-model workflows that improve code quality while controlling latency and cost.

Pattern 1: Cross-model verification ("LLM-as-a-Judge") in loop and graph workflows

When building agentic loops or multi-step graph workflows, using the same model to both write code and review its own output can reinforce model-specific blind spots. Pairing two distinct model families, one as the implementer and another as the validator (judge), provides independent verification before moving to the next stage of a workflow.

In Antigravity, you can run this pattern either interactively or via automated subagents:

  1. Plan and implement with Model A: Start in planning mode using Claude Opus 5.5 or Gemini 4 Argon to design and implement a multi-file change.
  2. Validate with Model B: Before committing or advancing the loop, switch models, or invoke a one-shot /model check in the CLI, to have a different model family critique the implementation against your test suite and requirements.

Pattern 2: Pairing reasoning models with Flash subagents

Complex engineering tasks often combine a few high-reasoning decisions with dozens of high-volume, mechanical lookups (searching files, grepping logs, checking lint output, or classifying test failures). Running every lookup on a frontier model can increase both latency and spend.

Antigravity's Subagent customization system (.agents/agents/*.md) lets you assign specific model tiers (inherit, flash, or pro) to specialized subagents. When your primary session is running a more powerful model.

Subagents configured with model: inherit use your active session model for deep reasoning subtasks.

Subagents configured with model: flash offload high-speed search, classification, and triage work to Gemini Flash models.

For example, you can define a fast log-triage subagent in .agents/agents/test-triager.md:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '--- name: test-triager description: Runs unit tests, classifies failures, and returns a concise summary of failing assertions. model: flash tools: - read - edit --- Run the requested test targets, classify any failures by root cause (compilation error, assertion failure, or timeout), and return a structured summary to the parent agent.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7feadd3b4310>)])]>

And a cross-model code reviewer subagent in .agents/agents/gemini-judge.md:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "--- name:cross-model-judge description: Independent LLM-as-a-judge verifier that audits diffs and edge cases using Gemini Pro. model: pro tools: - read --- Review the current workspace diff against the user's requirements. Check for regressions, missing edge-case tests, and security issues. Output a pass/fail verdict with specific line references."), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7feadd368e90>)])]>

With this setup, you can delegate rapid test-and-classify loops to test-triager and trigger cross-model-judge to validate the final diff, combining the strengths of each model in a single workflow.

Getting started

Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 are available now for Google Cloud customers using Antigravity:

  1. Administrators (Gemini for business): Third-party partner models do not draw from the pooled Gemini Enterprise Standard and Plus edition monthly token quota. Instead, usage is billed on a pay-as-you-go basis through your existing Google Cloud Billing account, so overages must be enabled. Visit “Gemini Enterprise” > “Settings” > “AI developer tools” in the Google Cloud Console to configure overage billing, spend limits and authorize partner models for your organization. See Configure AI developer tools settings for step-by-step instructions.
  2. Administrators (Gemini platform): You can also enable partner models if you are using Antigravity through the API in Gemini platform. Enable Claude models in Model Garden and complete the standard Anthropic terms.
  3. Developers: Update to the latest version of Antigravity 2.0, the Antigravity CLI, or the Antigravity IDE extensions, and open the model picker (or run /model) to select the right model for your task. To learn more about enterprise governance and multi-agent configuration, visit the Google Antigravity Enterprise documentation. You can switch the active model between turns in the same conversation thread while preserving workspace state, open artifacts, and terminal context.

Note: Lightweight first-party Gemini models continue to run in the background to handle high-frequency client-side coordination, such as context management and summaries. They consume first-party tokens and can incur charges.

item.title: Introducing Gemini for government services
item.description:
Earlier this month at Gemini at Work, we introduced the Gemini agent: a single, universal agent for work. It answers your questions, handles your knowledge work, creates your images and media, and writes and runs code. You give it objectives, not instructions, and come back to finished work. It plans the work, uses skills and tools, connects to your systems, and has the security, administration, and governance your organization requires.

Every industry runs on knowledge a general model does not have. Government work runs on statute, regulation, and agency guidance, across siloed legacy systems, under strict requirements for data sovereignty, compliance, and confidentiality. Too often that leaves civil servants on data entry and manual document review instead of the services citizens depend on.

Today we're bringing the Gemini agent to public service with Gemini for government services in preview, part of our new suite of purpose-built industry solutions. It adds skills built around government work, connections to the systems agencies already run, and specialized partner agents, with governance running underneath it all.

Five components of Gemini for government services

Developed alongside agency leaders, Gemini for government services provides an integrated, fully governed environment configured for rapid deployment across federal, state, and local agencies with five core components:

  1. Skills for government work: Skills are reusable instructions and context, written by domain experts, that teach Gemini to run a specific task. Each one applies the statute, regulation, and agency guidance that govern that task, so an agency's standard operating procedures carry into the work Gemini supports.
  2. Connectors to agency systems: Secure connectors link Gemini to the case management, ERP, HR, and collaboration systems agencies already run, along with authoritative federal data sources. Gemini queries each system in place, so no data is migrated, and access follows the identity and permission controls the agency already has.
  3. Partner agents: Skills and connectors come together in agents, including pre-built agents from public sector software providers that agencies can deploy right away. They handle tasks like FOIA discovery and batch redaction under the same central governance, with a person approving each consequential step.
  4. A governed control plane: Security and compliance teams get one place to set and enforce policy across every agent, including VPC Service Controls, CMEK, and Assured Workloads. Outputs are grounded in source documents, with citations, so reviewers can check where each answer came from.
  5. An open partner ecosystem: Every agency works under a different statute and runs a different mix of systems. System integrators and public sector ISVs help agencies customize Gemini, connect it to what they already have, and scale it without lock-in.

Skills for government workflows

Gemini for government services helps automate and accelerate complex government operations, including:

  • Policy and regulatory research: Ask an operational or eligibility question and get an answer drawn from the CFR, the Federal Register, state administrative codes, and internal manuals, with page and paragraph citations. Where federal and state rules both apply, Gemini shows which one governs to empower agency decision makers.
  • FOIA record discovery: Gemini searches SharePoint, Drive, and email archives for records responsive to a FOIA or state Sunshine Law request. It organizes them into a review set for the records officer and agency counsel, shortening discovery that often takes weeks.
  • Redaction for public release: Gemini finds sensitive constituent data across a batch of documents, groups the findings so reviewers can clear them in passes, and proposes redactions labeled by statutory exemption. After a reviewer confirms, it produces the exemption log and audit-ready copies.
  • Vendor bid evaluation: Gemini checks multi-volume bids against RFP requirements, FAR guidelines, minimum mandatory criteria, and evaluation rubrics, and returns scoring justifications with citations. Contracting officers get a documented basis for each award decision.
  • Grant and program expense audits: Gemini checks invoices, receipts, purchase orders, and ledger entries against 2 CFR 200 Uniform Guidance and the terms of the award. It flags unallowable costs, missing documentation, and funding discrepancies with line-item citations, so problems surface while there's still time to fix them.
  • Document validation at intake: Gemini classifies and validates pay stubs, W-2s, utility bills, and leases when they arrive, checks the numbers for consistency, and flags missing signatures. Defects are caught before the application enters the queue, not weeks into the case.
  • Plain-language notices: Gemini turns policy memos and agency guidance into public notices, aligned to the Plain Writing Act of 2010, USDA-FNS standards, and Title VI language access guidance.

Open ecosystem of connectors across the government technology stack

Gemini for government services connects directly to core agency systems via secure connectors. Access is bound by existing role-based access controls, record-level permissions, and the trusted data controls inherited from each system — and nothing is migrated to make the connection work.

Federal regulatory and public data:

  • Federal Register: Tracks legislative actions, regulations, and executive orders as they post, so state and local teams see federal changes as they land.
  • regulations.gov: Tracks federal rulemaking dockets, public comments, and statutory agency response deadlines, keeping policy analysts ahead of incoming mandates.
  • eCFR (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations): Grounds answers in the governing regulation, with citations down to the paragraph.

Agency systems of record:

  • Oracle E-Business Suite: Gives agents permission-bound access to procurement, payables, and ledger transactions for expense auditing and award reconciliation.
  • Oracle PeopleSoft: Connects HR and personnel records under existing role-based controls, so workforce questions are answered from the system of record.
  • Salesforce: Enables conversational experiences across the Missionforce portfolio through headless integration with Gemini, including benefits, licensing, permitting, and contact center management.
  • ServiceNow: Automates IT, CRM, security, employee experience, and workflow records, so agents can track incidents, requests, and approval chains inside existing routing rules.

Productivity and collaboration:

  • Google Workspace: Connects with Google Docs, Gmail, Drive, and Sheets to analyze case communications and agency correspondence and surface internal files while enforcing agency access controls.
  • Microsoft 365 and SharePoint: Integrates with Word, Outlook, and SharePoint to triage inquiries and ground responses in mail and intranet repositories without breaking workflow context.

Third-party agents and implementation partners

Every agency operates differently. Through our open platform, agencies can deploy pre-built partner agents or work with system integrators to scale custom capabilities:

  • SZNS Solutions FOIA and public records discovery agent: Turns a plain-language request, a piece of correspondence, or a formal citizen inquiry into a scoped search across enterprise archives — bounded by custodian and date range, so a records officer narrows the set before any data moves. It exports responsive material into secure agency repositories and tracks delivery status, giving each request an auditable trail from intake to release.
  • SZNS Solutions document redaction agent: Works inside connected repositories — SharePoint and Drive among them — finding sensitive citizen data across a batch and grouping the findings so a reviewer clears them in passes rather than page by page. Each proposed redaction carries its statutory exemption, and once the reviewer confirms, the agent exports permanently redacted, audit-ready copies back to the system of record, with the processing never leaving the agency's cloud perimeter.
  • Systems integrators & tech partners: Strategic partnerships with Accenture Federal Services, Clutch, Dark Wolf, Daston, Deloitte, Egen, Game Plan Tech, Knexus, Onix, Resultant, SAIC, Slalom, and SZNS Solutions so agencies can customize, integrate, and scale these capabilities without vendor lock-in.

Developed alongside federal, state, and local government agencies

We are working closely with select federal and state agencies, including the State of Missouri and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to ensure these capabilities work in day-to-day agency operations.

"Our citizens expect the government to move at the speed of modern life, not the speed of paperwork. By automating routine work in our workflows, we're delivering faster, better services to Missourians." - Tim Marczewski, Director of AI and Innovation, State of Missouri Office of Administration.

Built on an enterprise-grade foundation

Gemini for government services runs on Google Cloud's secure foundation, and can be deployed using the Assured Workloads FedRAMP High Data Boundary, enforcing U.S. data residency and personnel controls. It works within the authorities, retention rules, and approval chains your agency already has.

Agency records, constituent data, institutional documents, custom agents, and model outputs stay private to your organization, and are never used to train or fine-tune Google's foundation models without your permission. Because we operate the full stack, from infrastructure and models through the application layer, we can tune performance and cost together — routing high-volume document parsing and routine records sweeps to fast, low-cost models and reserving high-reasoning models for complex policy analysis, so expanding what your teams can take on does not mean expanding spend at the same rate.

This is just the beginning

The launch of Gemini for government services represents another defining step in delivering on our promise to bring the best of Gemini to every professional, for every workflow, natively tailored to the way they work.

Gemini for government services is available in preview today, joining our purpose-built solutions for industries. We invite leaders at every level of government to explore how Gemini can transform their most critical workflows.

item.title: Building full virtual vehicles on Google Cloud: From AAOS to the smallest MCU
item.description:
Imagining traditional gearheads getting their hands on software-defined vehicles is an amusing thought experiment. With their socket wrenches and air compressors at the ready, they might be confused to encounter core functions more likely to run on 1s and 0s than oil and belts. But across the auto industry these days, more and more vehicles feature prominent systems built using cloud-native development, continuous integration/continuous delivery, fast digital iteration, and plenty of AI.

But there’s still a big gap to be found in many automakers’ and Tier 1 suppliers’ cloud-based development processes. On the one hand, these companies are commonly using software to develop vehicles’ digital entertainment and information screens, or other onboard high-performance computers. 

On the other, the dozens of microchips and control modules that make a car a car these days — such as gateways, body controllers, zone control units, sensor and actuator nodes — are still frequently hardwired to physical chips when they’re constructed, making them very difficult to update, reprogram, or expand after the vehicle drives off the factory floor. Teams have to wait for benches, samples, and rigs, and integration can easily slip to the end of the development process, where defects are most expensive to fix.

This inherent inefficiency has become a leading bottleneck. After all, manufacturers can’t really claim vehicles are software-defined if most of their electronics only function when connected to physical hardware and if developers are leaning heavily on actual hardware.

With Horizon, our agentic innovation platform for developing software-defined vehicles, our vision is to help manufacturers avoid these inefficiencies by working with partners like RemotiveLabs.

The cockpit already runs in the cloud

The Android team has invested a significant amount of time and effort over the last few years on enabling seamless development of the many digital systems in vehicles’ cockpits. Android Automotive OS (AAOS) runs inside Google’s official virtual testing environment for Android, Cuttlefish, which itself runs comfortably on Arm-based Google Cloud instances. With this approach, developers can build, boot, and test virtual versions of their infotainment stacks on the same Arm architecture that ships in vehicles.

And with the recent launch of Android 17 and AAOS SDV, this capability is also extended to further domains, whenever AAOS SDV is used. Deploying it with Cuttlefish, for example, proves the model: representative software, on representative architecture, in the cloud, on demand. The question that still needs to be answered is how to extend that model to the rest of the vehicle, especially when other operating systems are involved.

The harness around the virtual vehicle

That’s where RemotiveTopology comes into play. As the harness around the virtual vehicle, it’s the layer that connects AAOS in Cuttlefish to a full, simulated electrical and electronic (E/E) architecture: the rest of the vehicle’s onboard computers, its data networks, and the live signals that make the system function like a real vehicle rather than a collection of standalone apps.

RemotiveTopology automatically utilizes manufacturers’ existing network design files to build a working, virtual version of their cars’ networks. This is vehicle-as-code: the E/E architecture expressed as an executable specification, versioned and provisioned like infrastructure-as-code. In this way, an entire vehicle can be spun up on demand. Cockpit software talks to the rest of the vehicle exactly as it would in a real vehicle. As a result, developers get full and continuous signal and cross-domain visibility, so they can see real-time system status. And because it is built on standard Linux tooling, the same topology runs on a laptop and in a contiguous integration pipeline on Google Cloud.

Integrate across domains early, not late

The payoff for using this approach is that all onboard systems can be developed and integrated with software before any of them are connected to a vehicle’s hardware. That’s beneficial because the most difficult (and latest) integration in a vehicle’s development is bringing all its systems together. For example, advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) produce object lists, trajectories, and mode requests that the cockpit has to render and react to, while the infotainment system and information cluster have to reflect driving state while body and chassis nodes sit in the loop.

With the full topology live on Google Cloud, the infotainment system and ADAS can operate simultaneously within a virtual vehicle, exchanging real signals over the simulated network. This means it’s possible to exercise handoffs like an ADAS event surfacing in the cluster or a driver-mode change rippling across domains from day one in continuous integration long before the benches and samples line up. In this way, developers can be confident they’ll discover multi-domain integration long before the end of the process so that they can test continuously from the start.

The full vehicle frontier

At the heart of this work is a shared desire to bring scalable software development to even the smallest and most common nodes in a vehicle, its microchips and control modules. That’s because these are the parts that have traditionally been wired to hardware, and as a result are the biggest blocker to fully software-defined vehicles.

The ultimate goal is that the same software that runs in the cloud can run on vehicles’ actual control modules with no re-tooling or re-validation needed to move between them. That parity is natural with Arm-based Google Cloud infrastructure because the cloud and the car share an instruction set. Google's Axion makes it straightforward: C4A metal, a bare-metal Arm instance, is provided explicitly for automotive systems development and Android software development, giving direct hardware access without unnecessary software layers and delivering the consistent performance that vehicle systems require.

Taken together, this holistic system allows teams, for the first time, to develop and integration-test an entire vehicle’s systems in the cloud and then apply it to the actual vehicle without having to rewrite it.

Why now, and where to start

The payoff is not abstract. Treating the vehicle as code and moving integration into the cloud compresses the slowest, most expensive phase of a program. Early customer engagements with RemotiveLabs have measured more than 10x faster integration cycles. And the development loop is now changing faster than the hardware loop: AI-assisted and agentic workflows can rapidly generate, test, and refine vehicle software, but only virtual systems provide the required scale. Every element that can’t be virtualized can slow the entire development process down.

RemotiveTopology provides this architecture as vehicle-as-code and makes it accessible for developers, testers, and autonomous AI agents alike. Best of all, there is no new third-party tooling to adopt just to get started. Instead, RemotiveLabs publishes an open-source simplified vehicle on GitHub that anyone can run in minutes on standard Linux tooling and platform definitions already in place. Full existing toolchains plug in as a manufacturer or Tier1 supplier scales, and RemotiveTopology can be easily dropped into an Arm-based Google Cloud environment.

For those building software-defined vehicles whose virtual development stops at the cockpit, it’s time to start with an open-source example, bring unique platform definitions, and run an entire vehicle in the cloud. RemotiveTopology is available in Horizon for easy usage in combination with other Horizon modules.

item.title: Who judges the judge? Three helpful ways to audit your LLM evaluators
item.description:
Is your LLM-as-a-judge truly objective? 

There’s a common misconception in tech that humans are subjective, so we should rely on AI for objective evaluation. But the reality is that LLMs are also subjective. Just like human reviewers, they can carry biases:

  • Verbosity bias: LLM judges usually favor longer, confident-sounding answers, even when the underlying facts are wrong.
  • Position bias: Swapping the order of two options can cause an LLM judge to flip its verdict over 75% of the time.
  • The halo effect: Because LLMs generate text piece by piece, clean grammar and formatting can trick an AI judge into giving top marks for accuracy while missing errors.
  • Agreeableness bias: LLM judges are great at recognizing valid work. But with detecting errors, they may fail to catch incorrect, buggy, or unsafe outputs up to 75% of the time.
  • Self-enhancement bias: Also known as egocentric bias, AI evaluators systematically overrate outputs that were generated by themselves or from their own family.

Ultimately, LLM judges are not objective arbiters of truth. They are subjective models with their own distinct biases. Treating them as infallible tools that don't need their quality measured might leave your work compromised. 

In this post, we’ll explore what’s holding enterprises back from strong evals, and share an easy three-pillar method you can use to improve your quality. 

Three helpful ways to audit your LLM judges 

Pillar 1: Measure internal stability

Before you can trust an AI judge’s score, you need to know that it isn't just guessing. Because LLMs are probabilistic, they can be inconsistent, giving different scores to the exact same text.

You can test this internal stability by running multi-pass consistency checks on a single output and calculating the variance. If a judge's scores fluctuate wildly on identical inputs, its rubric is too ambiguous.

Pillar 2: Validate human alignment

When your evaluation datasets are mostly valid responses, a lenient AI judge can look great on paper. It might align closely with human reviewers overall, but miss a majority of invalid or even unsafe outputs.

To prove your LLM judge is catching real errors, you need chance-corrected metrics. These mathematical models filter out agreements driven purely by leniency or random chance, showing how closely your evaluator actually aligns with the informed decisions of human experts.

Pillar 3: Use multi-judge ensembles

To avoid the halo effect mentioned earlier, teams should use decomposed prompting. Instead of asking one LLM judge to score an entire response, assign a specialized judge to evaluate a single criteria, like factual accuracy or tone. This isolates traits and forces independent scoring.

Second, to track performance in real time without human intervention, the established best practice is ensembling. This means running at least two different models under the hood to evaluate the exact same output simultaneously. 

By finding the statistical consensus between these models, you can flag if their evaluations begin to diverge and avoid any scoring quality degradation.

item.title: Four evaluation engineering lessons learned from building agent plugins
item.description:
The real challenge of building an agentic system isn't the construction, it's the measurement. 

Evaluation engineering is a critical foundation for building reliable AI systems. Setting up systematic, repeatable tests to measure your agent’s true behavior can be the difference between shipping a tool you can trust and one that silently breaks, fails to call APIs, or makes mistakes. 

I’ve run evaluation engineering initiatives for years at Google and developing the newly released Google Cloud Developer plugin served as a live testbed to stress-test these key principles across real-world developer workflows.

Here are four eval lessons we learned from building the new plugin that you can apply to your own builds.

1. Grade the execution steps instead of the summary

When we first evaluated agents, we set up an LLM-as-judge to inspect the agent’s final text reply and scored it against a checklist. However, we quickly realized it’s fundamentally flawed because the grader only sees what the agent wrote, not what it actually did. When we ran our initial 11-prompt evaluation suite for the Google Cloud Developer plugin, the automated grader marked it as failing three prompts. But when we opened the raw tool-call logs and read the transcripts, the plugin had actually passed all three. On a Cloud Run cleanup prompt, for instance, our rubric required checking command syntax before running anything. The agent ran gcloud help run services list as its very first step. It did the work, but its final message was focused on warning the user about permanent data loss rather than reciting that it had checked the help docs.

The grader penalized the agent for doing the right thing simply because it didn’t brag about it in the summary. If your rubric line says "did it run X?", a LLM judge is guessing unless you evaluate the actual tool-call trajectory.

Takeaway: Don't grade an agent on its closing pitch. Score the raw execution trajectory to verify what commands were actually executed, validated, and scoped.

2. Design evals for asynchronous operations

When you start reading tool-call trajectories, how you extract that telemetry matters just as much as what you're reading. Extracting agent telemetry into a flattened, sequential list of events obscures concurrent tool dispatch, which is one of the critical causes of behavioral failure. Modern agent harnesses often batch multiple tool invocations into a single assistant turn using an array of calls.

In our evaluations, when an agent was asked to inspect an environment and look up documentation, the harness dispatched the skill-loading call and two documentation searches simultaneously within a single tool_calls payload. Because activating a skill is a multi-stage process, where the initial call returns a short launch stub and the subsequent turn injects the full instruction body, the instructions meant to govern the search arrived in the prompt context after the system had already executed the searches.

The system never gave the skill a dedicated turn to let its guidance influence the agent's actions. If telemetry pipelines strip out turn structures and merge calls into a flat timeline, engineers will waste days wondering why an agent disregarded unambiguous instructions that a developer embedded in a skill.

Takeaway: Preserve turn structure in telemetry extractors so you can identify when client-side parallel dispatch issues tool calls before injected guidance enters the context window. 

3. Test live runs and "dry runs" side-by-side

You need to inspect real API calls to catch harness quirks, like parallel dispatch. But if you only test your agent in one environment condition, you're flying half-blind. From day one, you need to run two conditions side-by-side: a live run and a plan-only run. In the live condition, the agent has real, sandboxed credentials and actually executes commands. This is how you see if syntax works, parameters serialize cleanly, and the agent exercises restraint before doing something destructive. 

Live runs frequently hit an unexpected permission error on step two and abort before you ever reach the behavior you’re trying to test. That's why you need the plan-only condition, where you strip credentials and tell the agent to explain what it would do without running anything. This strips out permission roadblocks and shows you the model’s pure reasoning and routing intent. Roughly half our most important findings came from the delta between the two.

For example, on one of our onboarding prompts, a live run was blocked immediately on a project list call. The plan-only run sailed right through and produced an 8,000-character plan that completely ignored organization policies, admin approvals, and governance. The live run masked a major cognitive flaw that the plan-only run exposed in seconds.

Takeaway: Run live and plan-only evaluations side by side. Live runs test actual execution and safety restraint; plan-only runs expose the model's raw reasoning and routing without getting tripped up by permission errors.

4. Use “golden sets” as durable baselines

Frontier model architectures change every few months, agent harnesses improve, and plugin manifest standards will inevitably evolve. When building the Google Cloud Developer plugin, we treated evaluations as continuous integration testing for these non-deterministic environments. That means we stress-tested the composite stack, including the harness, the live model, and the tools running together on realistic tasks.

Instead of guessing from the final text output, this approach captures the whole trajectory: what the agent thought, what commands it actually ran, and whether it solved the problem without breaking anything. Then you score that run against golden sets curated by real human experts who know what the ideal path looks like.

Takeaway: Build golden sets based on what the entire system should actually do in the wild, including your harness, model, and plugins. Models change, but those baseline runs are your safety net.

Reminder: Use evaluation suites over “one-shot” demos

A common mistake I see among engineers is what I like to call the one-shot demo. This is when someone feeds a prompt into a LLM, watches it build a complete 3D game or solves a Rubik’s cube in a single pass and calls it an eval. But in reality, this is just a vanity metric. 

To do quality work with AI, I truly believe that you need evaluation suites. Without evaluations, teams are like literally running into a dark cave blind. Engineering an enterprise-grade agent means testing the system's ability to handle multi-step interactions, manage permissions, and avoid destructive outcomes like accidentally deleting a project because you asked it to "find opportunities to save costs."

Where to go from here

Building an agent plugin or MCP server is the beginning. Shipping something you can actually trust with real cloud infrastructure requires significantly more work in evaluations to ensure it’s doing what you expect it to do. At the end of the day, the only thing that outlasts model churn is a stress-tested eval suite. Check out the Google Cloud Developer plugin documentation or explore this codelab to get started with the plugin in Antigravity.

item.title: Architecting autonomy: A design pattern for high-compute, governed agents in biotech
item.description:
In production systems today, most AI agents operate as lightweight dispatchers. They parse a prompt, make an API call, retrieve a record, and hand back control. Their execution is fast, stateless and cheap. Biotechnology does not work this way. 

Folding a protein target, screening a 50,000 compound ligand library, or evaluating structure-activity relationships (SAR) are not quick API lookups. They are sustained, stateful, GPU-bound simulations that run for minutes or even hours across specialized silicon. When you ask a general-purpose large language model (LLM) endpoint to coordinate a complex drug discovery workflow, the standard paradigm breaks: Timeouts occur, context windows overflow with atomic coordinates, and proprietary chemical Intellectual Property (IP) risks exposure to external networks. 

Building enterprise grade research and development (R&D) agents requires moving past the monolithic assistant model. In this blog post, we will discuss how to use a three-layer architecture: separating cognitive orchestration (the brain) from computational execution (the muscle), and anchoring both inside an enterprise governance plane to build scalable agents for drug discovery use cases in biotech.

A three-layer pattern

The reference architecture below shows how to architect, optimize, and govern high-compute autonomous agents in biotechnology, specifically Drug Discovery.

The execution layer: scaling the muscle - high-compute execution 

The execution layer is responsible for the heavy scientific computations. The first architectural decision is determining where workloads should run:

  • Strategic, proprietary pipelines require dedicated GPU infrastructure within your security perimeter

  • Routine or standardized workloads can safely be delegated to managed cloud endpoints

In this architecture, protein folding is driven by ESMFold and generative design by GenMol. Both run as NVIDIA Inference Microservices or NIMs deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) using G4 VMs backed by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs.

A critical hurdle in containerized GPU workloads is the cold-start penalty, the latency delay required to pull multi-gigabyte model weights from an image registry and stage them into GPU memory (VRAM).

To ensure low latency responsiveness, we build the following as a recommendation into the reference architecture:

  • Maintain warm pools: Pin the GKE node pool to a minimum of one active node.

  • Preload weights: Model weights are loaded directly into VRAM at pod initialization, ensuring containers are immediately ready for inference.

  • Resilient scheduling: GKE manages pod lifecycles and restarts failed instances without tearing down the underlying VM infrastructure. 

This approach trades custom, manual CUDA kernel tuning for NVIDIA's pre-compiled, containerized runtimes, dramatically reducing infrastructure engineering overhead while ensuring deterministic throughput.

In biotech, chemical structures represent millions of dollars in proprietary IP. A docking request transmits SMILE strings or 3D coordinate matrices that must never leave company custody.

Containerized NIMs eliminate the friction between rapid prototyping and rigorous data isolation. During early exploration, researchers can query NVIDIA hosted endpoints. When transitioning to proprietary lead candidates, the exact same container is deployed to GKE inside a private VPC. The agent’s orchestration logic remains identical; only the target URI updates from an external proxy to an internal VPC endpoint. No structural data leaves the enterprise perimeter.

The cognitive layer: Multi-agent reasoning

With compute execution isolated, the cognitive layer manages agentic workflow sequencing. Built on Agent Runtime, within the Gemini platform, this reference architecture shows a system that deploys a hierarchical multi-agent structure, one lead orchestrator, and two specialized domain sub-agents (Lead Optimization and Safety Screening) . The multi-agent design can be modified to suit the use case at hand. 

Based on this design, when an end-user submits a high-level task such as “ Analyze Candidate 4b against Target X and produce a SAR report”, the system applies four core orchestration patterns discussed below; 

  • In-process native agent handoffs: The lead orchestrator delegates tasks to specialist sub-agents using Agent Runtime’s native SDK rather than network-serialized agent-to-agent HTTP protocols. This eliminates intermediate network hops and keeps internal handoffs instantaneous. Only the outermost boundary communicates outward to user-facing surfaces like the Gemini agent.
  • Passing bulky payloads by reference: LLMs degrade quickly when forced to ingest massive arrays of 3D spatial coordinates. In this architecture, raw structural data (PDB files, docking poses, trajectory logs) is written directly to Cloud Storage. Agents pass lightweight, signed object URIs and high-level structural summaries, keeping context windows compact and inference costs down.
  • Decoupling workflow logic from biochemical reasoning: General-purpose LLMs excel at task planning and synthesis, but are prone to hallucinating biochemical nuances. To control this behavior, this architecture maintains strong separation of concerns, namely, workflow and tasks decomposition are handled by Gemini. Domain chemistry and pharmacological reasoning are handled by specialized Nemotron models hosted on dedicated GPU nodes. 
  • Context-driven evaluation over rigid cutoffs: Traditional computational screening enforces arbitrary numerical cutoffs (e.g., discard if binding affinity ,-7.5 kcal/mol) However, therapeutic context fundamentally alters risk tolerance. Preventive cardiovascular therapy taken daily by healthy patients requires extremely strict safety margins, or a novel oncology candidate targeting an intractable cancer may accept higher toxicity if efficacy is demonstrated.

By passing disease context directly into the specialized reasoning models, drug candidates are evaluated against dynamic, target-specific profiles rather than static thresholds, preventing the premature culling of viable drug leads.

Performance best practices for high-compute pipelines

Optimizing an agentic system that interfaces with heavy GPU compute requires challenging common engineering instincts:

Common Assumption

Architectural Reality

Recommended Best Practice

"Swap in a faster driver model to cut latency."

The primary orchestrator's token generation is rarely the bottleneck in multi-step R&D pipelines.

Optimize I/O, not token speed: Focus on reducing payload sizes and intermediate network hops rather than compromising orchestrator reasoning depth.

"Parallelize tool calls across workers."

External scientific services and containerized models often serialize requests internally on dedicated hardware.

Respect execution topology: Align client-side concurrency with backend queue mechanics to prevent pipeline lockouts and connection timeouts.

"Pass full simulation states between tools."

Large JSON bodies cause schema validation failures, prompt truncation, and token bloat.

Pass heavy payloads by reference: Store raw coordinates in object storage and pass lightweight URIs between agent boundaries.

"Return outputs only when the pipeline finishes."

Long multi-minute runs leave scientists blind to whether jobs are proceeding or stalled.

Stream intermediate stage completions: Emit progress updates at each completed milestone (e.g., folding complete, docking running) for real-time visibility.

"Chain multiple granular micro-tools."

Deep tool-chains increase the probability of hallucinated arguments and schema mismatches.

Collapse compute pipelines: Wrap end-to-end simulation pipelines behind a single, clean tool interface that takes clear parameters and returns a consolidated object.

The enterprise governance and asymmetric autonomy

Deploying high-compute agents in enterprise environments requires robust data sovereignty, audit trails, and process control. The Gemini platform establishes these safeguards natively with the following components: 

  • Agent Identity: Every autonomous agent operates with a cryptographically verifiable identity. Thus, for a biotech use case, when a candidate molecule is advanced or rejected, the event is permanently logged to that specific agent principal. 

  • Agent Gateway: This serves the single ingress/egress point for every interaction within the perimeter. Centralized IAM and regional residency rules help ensure sensitive molecular data remains within designated cloud regions. 

  • Agent Registry: This feature maintains a curated catalog of approved agents, validated tool schemas, and authorized Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, preventing rogue tools from executing in production. 

  • Model Armor: This functionality inspects incoming prompts and outgoing payloads in real time to prevent prompt injection and data exfiltration. 

The payoff is clear. Identity, RBAC, auditing, residency, and data protection are native properties of the Gemini platform; this allows enterprise customers to focus on science rather than having to build a compliance stack for every project. 

In high-stakes research and development, full autonomy introduces unacceptable liability, while requiring approval for trivial steps can create frictions. The solution addressing this to use asymmetric gating in the following ways;

Automate reversible operations: For example, allow the agent to resolve chemical naming synonyms, pull structural PDBs, and run preliminary Lipinski screens autonomously without interrupting the researcher.

Gate irreversible operations: For instance, initiating multi-GPU docking run, advancing a lead compound to wet-lab synthesis, or archiving a therapeutic program must require explicit human sign-off.

The pattern, and the path forward

High-compute autonomous agents succeed when the boundaries between cognitive planning, numerical computation, and system governance are clean in the following ways:

  1. Keep the orchestrator focused on decomposition and synthesis, leaving intensive biophysical simulation to specialized, containerized microservices and models.

  2. Eliminate context bloat by passing complex chemical data by reference through cloud storage.

  3. Anchor the workflow in enterprise governance, pairing cryptographic agent identity with asymmetric human oversight.

As generative and structural biology models expand toward whole-cell modeling and complex dynamic simulations, this decoupled architecture ensures research systems scale efficiently while keeping proprietary IP secure and auditable.

item.title: How Visko streams real-time world models on Google Cloud TPUs
item.description:
Editor's note: Generative AI startups are moving rapidly beyond static clip generation to build interactive, real-time worlds. In this technical deep dive, we explore how AI startup Visko collaborated with Google Cloud TPU engineers to deploy Orbis — its continuously streaming Live World Model—on Cloud TPUs, going from initial kickoff to production handover in just 30 days.

What makes a live video world model so challenging to serve in production? The bottleneck isn't average throughput — it's beating a relentless real-time clock. Unlike offline video generators where a user submits a prompt and waits in a queue, a live world model streams continuously. Every new chunk of video and synchronized audio must finish rendering before the viewer finishes watching the previous one, or the world freezes.

Today, we're excited to share how Visko, an AI startup pioneering interactive world models, teamed up with Google Cloud to solve this exact challenge. Working side by side, Visko and Google Cloud engineers deployed Visko's end-to-end live inference pipeline — combining video generation, super-resolution upscaling, and synchronized audio—onto a single Cloud TPU slice. Together, the teams brought end-to-end generation down, rendering at 1.07x playback speed.

Here is an inside look at how we engineered the pipeline to hit that milestone in a single month, the architectural optimizations that moved the needle, and practical lessons for other startups building ultra-low-latency generative AI on Google Cloud.

Redefining interactive media with Live World Models

While most generative video platforms focus on rendering fixed, pre-baked clips, Visko is building what it calls Live Models: video world models that generate continuously and respond on the fly.

Visko's flagship model, Orbis, streams live video starting from a single text or image prompt. As the stream plays, viewers can enter new steering prompts in real time, dynamically evolving the scene without restarting or breaking continuity. For instance, in one test session, the livestream opens on a cat napping beside a crackling fireplace; when the viewer steers the scene to introduce a bowl of food, the bowl materializes seamlessly, and the cat stretches, stands up, and meows.

Since launching its public demo on September 1, 2026, Orbis has unlocked new possibilities across interactive entertainment, live commerce, AI companions, immersive education, and robotics simulation. To scale these interactive sessions reliably, Visko partnered with Google Cloud TPU engineers in August 2026 to port the Orbis live pipeline to Google's Tensor Processing Unit (TPU). Within 30 days, the full multimodal pipeline was running in real time on TPUs.

Visko’s ambition is to power a new generation of interactive worlds that people can step into and shape in real time. Streaming continuous video and audio under a strict clock is a fundamentally different system challenge than offline clip generation. Working side by side with Google Cloud's TPU engineers, we brought the full Orbis pipeline to TPUs in just 30 days — giving us the low-latency compute and memory bandwidth required to bring Live Models to creators and developers at scale.

"Visko is bringing an exciting new class of real-time, steerable workloads to the Cloud TPU ecosystem. By co-engineering their live multimodal pipeline on a singleTPU slice using JAX, torchax, and custom Pallas kernels, we proved how quickly a lean startup team can go from PyTorch prototype to render at 1.07x playback speed on Google Cloud's AI Hypercomputer."
– Dave Elliott, Head of Developer Advocacy for AI, Google Cloud 

Live video is a hard-deadline problem

When you serve an offline clip generator, latency is forgiving — the user waits once while the backend processes frames. A live world model has no waiting room.

Every single chunk must be denoised, decoded from latents, upscaled to 1664x936 (at 18 fps), and paired with generated audio faster than realtime playback speed, for as long as the session runs.

Two structural constraints make live world models far more demanding than standard batch inference:

  • Batch size of one: Each live stream represents an individual viewer's interactive session. You cannot mask latency by grouping dozens of concurrent requests into a massive batch — the standard playbook for keeping AI accelerators saturated.

  • Strict sequential dependency: Every chunk depends directly on the one before it. Because the video model maintains a rolling memory of recent video latents so that chunk N+1 smoothly continues the action from chunk N, you cannot pre-render chunks out of order or parallelize across future timestamps.

For startup infrastructure engineers coming from LLM serving, it helps to think of live world modeling not as a tokens-per-second throughput benchmark, but as an unforgiving per-step latency SLO.

Architecting the multimodal pipeline on a single TPU slice

To keep infrastructure lean and cost-effective as Visko scales, the team designed the live pipeline to chain three distinct generative models on a single Cloud TPU slice running in BF16 precision.

When a viewer submits an initial prompt or a live steering update, all three generative models — the core video diffusion model, the super-resolution upscaler, and the audio generator — share the same chips, taking turns on the hardware for each chunk.

To combine rapid startup iteration with bare-metal accelerator speed, the software stack is built on three open-source pillars:

  • JAX: Google's high-performance Python array library for accelerators, compiled into optimized machine code by the XLA compiler.

  • torchax: An interoperability layer that runs PyTorch models directly on Cloud TPUs via JAX, enabling startup teams to bring existing PyTorch components over without an upfront, ground-up rewrite.

  • Pallas: The custom kernel programming language for TPUs in JAX.

Real-time performance breakdown: Hitting the clock 

By profiling and optimizing each stage on a single slice in BF16, the engineering team achieved a total per-chunk latency of under the target while — maintaining roughly 7% headroom to absorb variance during live streaming:

Because video denoising accounts for nearly two-thirds of the total compute budget, that stage became the primary focus of our kernel and parallelism optimizations.

Inside the stack: Three optimizations that unlocked real-time streaming

1. Ulysses context parallelism across all TPU chips

A video chunk expands into a massive sequence of spatiotemporal tokens inside the video transformer. To distribute that workload across the TPU chips at batch size 1, the team implemented Ulysses context parallelism.

Instead of splitting model weights, Ulysses splits the token sequence across chips. Immediately before the attention layer, a high-speed all-to-all interconnect exchange regroups the tensors so that each chip holds the entire video sequence, but only for one-quarter of the attention heads. After each chip computes attention over the full sequence for its assigned heads, a second all-to-all exchange restores the sequence-split layout for the feed-forward layers.

2. Custom Pallas splash attention from MaxDiffusion

To accelerate the attention computation itself, the team integrated a custom Pallas splash attention kernel from MaxDiffusion, Google Cloud's open-source reference library for diffusion models on Cloud TPU.

Splash attention brings FlashAttention-style tiling to TPU architecture: rather than materializing the full quadratic attention matrix in High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), it computes attention in compact tiles that remain inside ultra-fast on-chip VMEM. Startup teams can drop the exact kernel used in this port straight into their own pipelines via custom_splash_attention.py.

3. A 5.8x audio speedup by moving from torchax to pure JAX

We first brought all three Orbis models onto Cloud TPU with torchax, which runs PyTorch code on TPU through JAX and XLA without a rewrite. For the video and upscaling models, torchax paired with Pallas attention kernels met our latency target directly, and both stay in torchax in the final pipeline.

Only the audio model needed a rewrite. Moving the audio stage from torchax to native JAX made it 5.8x faster and brought the full pipeline under the playback deadline.

Field notes for AI builders: Cloud TPU lessons

Takeaways from tuning live multimodal inference on Cloud TPU:

  • Ulysses context parallelism for single stream video: At batch size 1, splitting the token sequence across chips with all-to-all interconnect exchanges was faster than both tensor parallelism and ring attention.
  • Native BF16 for continuous streams: FP8 quantization cuts memory bandwidth pressure, but small quantization errors build up across chunks in a continuous stream. Native BF16 kept visual quality intact within the latency budget.
  • Selective JAX ports: torchax kept the video and upscaling models in PyTorch, so the team only rewrote the audio bottleneck in native JAX.
  • XLA compilation caching: The first boot spends a few minutes compiling XLA graphs. Caching compiled artifacts brings worker restarts under a minute.

Building real-time generative models on Cloud TPU? Start here

If your startup is pushing the boundaries of live video, world models, or ultra-low-latency multimodal inference, you can build with the same toolkit that powered Visko's port:

  • Accelerate diffusion attention out of the box: Grab the open-source splash attention kernel used in this collaboration from MaxDiffusion, and explore the Pallas documentation to write custom TPU kernels.

  • Migrate PyTorch fast, then optimize selectively: Bring your existing PyTorch models onto TPU quickly with torchax, pinpoint bottlenecks with the Cloud TPU Profiler, and port latency-critical stages to native JAX.

  • Spin up TPUs on demand: Use TPU Flex-start VMs to provision TPU capacity for short development and benchmarking runs without a long-term reservation.

  • Scale with Google for Startups: Early-stage AI startups looking for cloud credits, technical mentorship, and access to Google Cloud's AI Hypercomputer stack can apply to the Google for Startups Cloud Program.

Special thanks to the Visko.ai team for the close technical partnership, and to the Google Cloud TPU engineers who lead the project including: Yixin Shi, James Huang, and Elisa Tsai.
